payload.content: {"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=metrics+and+frameworks+for+evaluating+research+problem+significance+in+autonomous+AI+agents&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.1007/978-3-032-26749-8_4\", \"title\": [\"Evaluating AI Agents\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-26749-8_4\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.20944/preprints202603.1694.v1\", \"title\": [\"A Brief History of AI for Scientific Discovery: Open Research, Metrics, and Autonomous Agents\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>The history of artificial intelligence for scientific discovery is not a two year story about chatbots learning to write papers. It is a sixty year story about science repeatedly handing its bottlenecks to machines—first inference, then search, then measurement, then the full workflow—only to discover that each delegation solves one problem and exposes a harder one underneath. This paper traces that history from DENDRAL (1965) through the construction of open scholarly infrastructure (arXiv, Google Scholar, ORCID), the oracle breakthroughs of AlphaFold, and the current era of LLM driven autonomous research agents. Three interlocking threads are followed including AI as research instrument, AI for research infrastructure, and the reshaping of scholarly profiles and incentives by machine readable metrics. The central tension throughout is between automation and augmentation between building systems that replace human researchers and tools that amplify human creativity and judgement. The paper presents that the most consequential development is not any single tool but the emergence of an interconnected ecosystem where AI agents, preprint platforms, open source codebases, and citation infrastructure form a feedback loop that is fundamentally restructuring who can do science, how fast discoveries propagate, and what counts as a valid scientific contribution.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202603.1694.v1\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 3, 23]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1007/978-3-032-26749-8\", \"title\": [\"Reliable Evaluations for LLMs and AI Agents\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-26749-8\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7508618\", \"title\": [\"AI-Assisted Software Engineering: Evaluating Copilot, Cursor, and Autonomous AI Agents for Rapid Application Development\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>The integration of large language models into software development tooling has produced a spectrum of assistance paradigms, from inline code completion to autonomous multi-step agents capable of navigating repositories and executing commands. This paper presents an empirical evaluation of three representative systems GitHub Copilot, Cursor, and autonomous agentic IDEs across a rapid application development task set. We assess effectiveness (does the generated application satisfy stated requirements?), efficiency (time to completion relative to unaided baselines), iteration behavior (error detection and corrective actions), and code quality outcomes (vulnerability rates, technical debt indicators). Our synthesis of controlled trials, enterprise telemetry studies, and standardized benchmarks finds a consistent pattern: AI assistance substantially accelerates low-complexity, high-boilerplate development tasks, but performance degrades sharply as task horizon and cross-file coherence requirements increase. Autonomous agents complete only a small fraction of end-to-end feature development tasks that short-horizon benchmarks suggest they can handle. Security vulnerability rates in generated code remain high across tools. We conclude with a practical framework for selecting assistance paradigms by task characteristics, and with an assessment of the gap between marketed capability and demonstrated capability.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7508618\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "66c02b324f4dbd49af930b19a2634622dd30dcb0547812a1d08a8f0ff55ca8b1", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "unassigned_problem", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.1007/978-3-032-26749-8_4", "doi:10.20944/preprints202603.1694.v1", "doi:10.1007/978-3-032-26749-8", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.7508618"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-26749-8_4", "https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202603.1694.v1", "https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-26749-8", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7508618"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
